status: candidate verdicts for operator review; not a gate
method_note: Each pair is judged against the six conditions of DISCREPANCY_BRIEF.md exactly as worded. Condition 4 asks that 'One study's estimate must lie outside the other's 95% interval'; where the exclusion holds in only one direction, or rests on a narrow margin, that is stated as fragility for the operator, not treated as a failed condition. Agreement between one paper's estimate and a figure that is NOT under the other paper's condition (another cohort, another model) is recorded as fragility, since only condition 3's matched figure dissolves a gap under the rule.

conditions_attacked.1_question: Holds. Both papers answer one question: what share of older people living with dementia in a high-income health system carry a diagnosis. P-1046 sets out 'to derive contemporary population-level diagnosis rates of MCI and dementia documented in the full Medicare population and compare these with the expected rates' (p. 2). P-977 defines 'People with dementia, who have received a diagnosis (diagnostic coverage)' (Figure 1.1, p. 16) and states 40-50% for 'most HIC' (p. 12). The population class is the same: older adults with dementia in high-income countries. The US is a high-income country, and P-977's sourced evidence on the point comes from primary-care studies 'conducted mainly in Europe and North America' (p. 33). The measurement channel is the same: clinical diagnosis records set against a cognitive-assessment prevalence. P-1046 compares ICD-coded claims with an HRS model built on the Langa-Kabeto-Weir cognitive classification (p. 3). P-977's Section 2.4 compares PCP judgement or notes with a research diagnostic assessment (p. 33). Country, era and data source are cohort and dataset differences, which condition 1 allows. The reader's objection is that P-977's headline is an unsourced generic assertion. That goes to its evidential weight, not to whether it addresses the same question. The rule has no sourcing condition, and the record reads the printed figure correctly.
conditions_attacked.2_metric: Holds. P-1046 defines its quantity as a proportion diagnosed: 'The O/E ratio can be interpreted as the proportion of expected cases that were diagnosed or the detection rate' (p. 3). It reads its MCI ratio directly as coverage ('of the estimated 8 million Medicare beneficiaries with MCI, 7.4 million were undiagnosed', p. 5). It also sets its dementia ratio against coverage estimates from other studies ('This dementia detection rate is much higher than the 38% reported by a meta-analysis of US-based studies prior to 2007 [29] and the July 2022 estimate of 62% from the National Health Service in England [30]', p. 6). The authors therefore treat their detection rate and a coverage proportion as one metric type. Their estimator can exceed 1 because its numerator counts every coded diagnosis. That is a case-ascertainment (label) difference, which the rule records as a candidate explanation, not a change of metric type. The reader's reconciliation needs 54-59% of claims diagnoses to fall outside the true case pool ((1.09-0.50)/1.09 = 0.54; (1.09-0.45)/1.09 = 0.59). That is a candidate explanation, and neither paper shows it is sufficient. P-1046 argues against it: it used 'a more stringent identification algorithm' and puts overdiagnosis at 'about 10%' (p. 6).
conditions_attacked.3_matched_figure: Holds. Neither paper reports the result under the other's condition. P-977 prints no figure for the US or for 2015-2019. P-1046 prints no figure for high-income countries in general or for the period before 2016. Every value P-1046 prints stays above 0.50: the three windows (1.086, 1.093, 1.104); its subgroups, including 'Others' at 0.630, which the reader's list of lowest subgroups omits, Black 0.696, Hispanic 0.758, age 65-69 0.831, dual-eligible 0.855 and Medicare Advantage 1.034; and its alternative denominators (0.096/0.113 = 0.85; 0.096/0.100 = 0.96). The 38% US figure that P-1046 cites comes from a third study. P-1046 cites it to say its own rate is 'much higher', which confirms the gap rather than dissolving it.
conditions_attacked.4_uncertainty: Holds in both directions. P-1046 prints no interval. Derived from its evaluation-set size, the observed rate is 0.095 on 41,205,474 beneficiaries, SE = sqrt(0.095 x 0.905 / 41,205,474) = 0.0000457, so O/E 1.104 has a sampling interval of 1.104-1.106. The expected rate comes from a model and adds more uncertainty. Bounding it with the HRS validation sample (observed dementia 0.078 on N = 9,808, SE = sqrt(0.078 x 0.922 / 9,808) = 0.0027, a relative 95% half-width of 6.8%) gives O/E of about 1.03-1.19. On the paper's own alternative denominators it is 0.85-0.96. P-977's 40-50% lies outside every one of these. In the other direction, P-977's sourced intervals both exclude 1.086-1.104 and also 0.85-0.96: diagnosis recorded in notes, 37.9% (26.8-49.6%), and PCP identification, 73.4% (62.6-82.9%). The difference is not one of significance only.
conditions_attacked.5_performance_validity: Not a performance comparison. The Section 3.5 exclusion does not apply.
conditions_attacked.6_record: Holds. The record has two defects: a P-1046 limitation quote ('underestimates true prevalence') that is not in the PDF, and P-977's HIC figure presented as sourced. Neither creates the disagreement. Both 1.086-1.104 and 40-50% are printed in the papers.

figures.P-1046: Dementia O/E 1.086, 1.093, 1.104 (2015-2017, 2016-2018, 2017-2019; 38,739,387 to 41,205,474 beneficiaries). Derived sampling interval for 1.104 is 1.104-1.106 (SE of the observed rate 0.0000457). Allowing for the HRS-model denominator (N = 9,808 validation, relative half-width 6.8%) gives about 1.03-1.19. On the paper's alternative US prevalence denominators, 0.85 (Rajan 0.113) and 0.96 (Manly 0.100). Lowest printed subgroup: 'Others' 0.630.
figures.P-977: 'In most HIC, only 40-50% of people living with dementia have received a diagnosis' (p. 12). No source, n or interval is printed for this figure, so none can be derived. Sourced figures from 15 primary-care studies 'mainly in Europe and North America': recorded in notes 37.9% (95% CI 26.8-49.6%); identified by PCPs 73.4% (62.6-82.9%) (p. 33).
figures.comparison: The 40-50% range lies outside every P-1046 interval above. P-977's sourced intervals exclude P-1046's 1.086-1.104, and 37.9% (26.8-49.6%) also excludes P-1046's lowest printed value (0.630). The two can coexist only if 54-59% of claims diagnoses fall outside the true case pool, a share neither paper measures.

results.not_shown_sufficient: No paper shows any of these explanations to be sufficient. P-1046 argues against the largest one (a numerator of mostly non-cases): it reports overdiagnosis of about 10% under its stricter algorithm and cites a linked HRS-Medicare estimate of 2.4%.
results.fragility: The P-977 side of the pair rests on an unsourced round range with no interval. The pair does not depend on it, though: P-977's sourced 37.9% (26.8-49.6%) recorded-diagnosis figure, from studies mainly in Europe and North America, independently excludes every value P-1046 prints.
results.reason: Both papers measure the share of people with dementia in high-income health systems who carry a diagnosis. P-1046 defines its O/E ratio as 'the proportion of expected cases that were diagnosed' and itself sets it against the 38% and 62% coverage figures, calling its rate 'much higher', so the question and the metric type are shared. The printed values (1.086-1.104, and never below 0.63 in any subgroup or 0.85 on any alternative denominator) lie outside P-977's 40-50% and outside its sourced intervals. No matched figure dissolves the gap. The coverage-versus-O/E construct, the model denominator and the era are candidate explanations that neither paper shows to be sufficient.

conditions_attacked.1_question: Holds on the incident estimate. The record's figures (RS1/RS2, 0.640 and 0.712) are prevalent-MCI AUCs, a misreading under condition 6, so the pair is judged on RS3 (0.785). RS3 is P-981's only incident-MCI figure and its abstract headline for conversion. Both papers predict incident MCI in cognitively normal, community-dwelling Chinese adults from baseline clinical, questionnaire and cognitive data, one channel. Label definition, predictors, cohort and validation design differ, and condition 1 allows all of these. Horizon is allowed too, and here it is closer than the reader implies. P-981 frames its own AUCs as predicting 'incident MCI in the subsequent 3–5 years based on baseline information' (p. 7), and P-824's 5-year figure falls within that framing. P-824 also reports that 'when the prediction time changed to 3 or 7 years, the result did not change substantially' (p. 7).
conditions_attacked.2_metric: Holds: ROC AUC on both sides (P-981 equates it with the c statistic).
conditions_attacked.3_matched_figure: Holds. The text prints no figure under the other paper's condition. P-824's 3-year AUCs appear only in Supplementary Figure 3 (an image with no numbers in the extract). What the text says about them ('did not change substantially') points away from reconciliation: shortening P-824's horizon toward P-981's does not move P-824's figure much. P-981's test-free scores on the incident sub-cohort appear only in Supplementary Table S1. P-824's CLHLS figure (0.797) agrees with 0.785, but it is not P-981's condition. It comes from another cohort (aged 65+, mean 80.9) with another label (CMMSE < 18), a cohort P-824 itself calls weak ('the predictive utility for MCI was relatively low in CLHLS'). It is a spread within P-824, not a matched figure.
conditions_attacked.4_uncertainty: Holds as worded, and in both directions at the like-for-like tier. Every figure is from Hanley-McNeil (HM). RS3 is apparent: it was fitted and scored on the same 921 people (72 converters, 849 stable). Q1 = 0.785/1.215 = 0.646 and Q2 = 2(0.616)/1.785 = 0.690, so SE = sqrt([0.169 + 71(0.030) + 848(0.074)]/(72 x 849)) = 0.0327, giving 0.721-0.849. P-824's CHARLS figure is also apparent, since the score was built in CHARLS: 0.861 with 2323/6470 events, SE 0.0051, giving 0.851-0.871. Each estimate lies outside the other's interval; z = 0.076/sqrt(0.0051^2 + 0.0327^2) = 2.30. The reader did not use one check. P-824 prints SEs for another model in the same cohorts (Supplementary Table 4: BDSI C index SE 0.011 in CHARLS, 0.020 in RuLAS). HM gives 0.0071 and 0.0224 for those, so the true-to-HM ratio is 1.56 in CHARLS and 0.89 in RuLAS. Scaled by these ratios, CHARLS is 0.861 +/- 1.96(0.0080) = 0.845-0.877, z = 2.26. Even taking 0.011 unscaled, CHARLS is 0.839-0.883, z = 2.20. The both-way exclusion survives the paper's own uncertainty scale. The record's own figure, RuLAS (external), is 0.823 with 260/391 events: HM gives 0.789-0.857 and the scaled SE (0.0157) gives 0.792-0.854. P-981's 0.785 lies outside by 0.004-0.007, one way only, since 0.823 lies inside RS3's interval. CLHLS shows no exclusion (z = 0.35). Condition 4 is met against CHARLS (both ways) and against RuLAS (one way).
conditions_attacked.5_performance_validity: Passes. No figure reaches 0.97. The highest is P-824's CHARLS 0.861, on 8,793 participants with two external cohorts. P-981's 0.785 is apparent on 72 events, so any optimism would lower it and widen the gap.
conditions_attacked.6_record: The record misreads P-981: RS1/RS2 are prevalent-MCI figures, not '~3-year incident MCI'. The pair is judged on the figure P-981 actually prints for incident MCI (RS3 0.785), as condition 6 directs.

results.not_shown_sufficient: No paper shows any explanation to be sufficient. For horizon, P-824 reports that its result did not change substantially at 3 years, which argues against horizon as the explanation.
results.fragility: The margins are narrow: 0.861 lies above RS3's HM upper bound (0.849) by 0.012, and 0.785 lies below RuLAS's lower bound by 0.004-0.007. The RS3 interval is an HM approximation on 72 events. One of P-824's three cohorts (CLHLS, 0.797) agrees with P-981. The operator may weigh that, but under the rule it is not a matched figure.
results.reason: On the figure P-981 actually prints for incident MCI (RS3, 0.785, apparent), the gap to P-824's apparent development estimate (0.861) exceeds uncertainty in both directions (z = 2.30). It stays at z = 2.20-2.26 when P-824's own printed SEs for another model in the same cohorts set the uncertainty scale. The record's comparator (RuLAS 0.823) also meets condition 4 as worded (0.785 outside 0.789-0.857). The CLHLS agreement is another cohort and label, not a figure under P-981's condition. Every condition is met. The label, predictor, horizon, event-count and cohort differences are not shown to be sufficient.

conditions_attacked.1_question: Holds (the reader agrees). Both papers model time to MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI MCI by Cox regression, with the MRI channel plus clinical and cognitive scales. P-13's high-risk subgroup (80.9% LMCI) is still Alzheimer's-spectrum MCI from ADNI, and a post hoc subgroup is a cohort-selection difference, which condition 1 allows. P-524, P-574 and P-940 carry no compared quantity.
conditions_attacked.3_matched_figure: Holds. P-1128's condition is a single-timepoint (baseline) input. P-13's only single-timepoint figures in the same subgroup are lower still ('in the baseline models, ADAS13 showed the best performance (C-index/Optimism-corrected C-index = 0.677/ 0.665)'), which widens the gap. P-13's low-risk baseline figure (0.825/0.793) comes from another subgroup. P-13 prints no C-index for its model in all MCI or at a 60-month horizon. P-1128 prints no subgroup C-index and no longitudinal model.
conditions_attacked.4_uncertainty: Holds as worded at both tiers, and in both directions at the headline tier. Headline against headline, both apparent: P-13's abstract gives 0.844 (95% CI 0.815-0.873), and P-1128's abstract gives its nomogram as 'C-index = 0.951' (Table 2 training interval 0.928-0.974). The printed intervals do not overlap. SEs from the printed intervals are 0.0148 and 0.0117, so z = 0.107/sqrt(0.0148^2 + 0.0117^2) = 5.67. This is the like-for-like comparison the record itself first drew ('a 0.107-point gap'). Its 'reconciliation' of P-1128's validation 0.880 against P-13's training 0.844 is the misreading condition 6 sets aside. Held out against held out: P-13's test-set 0.805 lies outside P-1128's printed validation interval (0.817-0.943), which is exactly condition 4's wording. In the other direction, HM over 30-70 converters in P-13's 103-person test split gives 0.703-0.722 to 0.888-0.907, which contains 0.880, so the held-out exclusion is one-way. The reader's own file says condition 4 'is met as worded' yet lists it as failed. Nothing in the rule makes a 'fairer tier' or a both-way test a requirement.
conditions_attacked.5_performance_validity: Passes. The highest figure is P-1128's training 0.951, below 0.97, and P-13's figures are 0.805-0.844.
conditions_attacked.6_record: The record's reconciliation compares figures that are not like for like (P-1128's validation against P-13's training). Judged on the printed figures, P-1128 is higher at both tiers, beyond the printed interval at each.

figures.P-13: High-risk subgroup (n = 340; split 237/103). Training C-index 0.844 (0.815-0.873; SE 0.0148). Optimism-corrected 0.829. Test 0.805, no interval; HM over 30-70 events of 103 gives SE 0.042-0.052 (50/53: 0.719-0.891).
figures.P-1128: n = 162 (68 converters within 6-60 months, 94 stable at 5 years; split 112/50). Network-morphology-clinical model: training 0.951 (0.928-0.974; SE 0.0117), validation 0.880 (0.817-0.943; SE 0.032).
figures.comparison: Training against training: disjoint intervals, z = 5.67. Held out against held out: 0.805 below P-1128's printed 0.817-0.943 by 0.012 (one-way); z = 0.075/sqrt(0.0437^2 + 0.032^2) = 1.4.

results.not_shown_sufficient: No paper shows any of these explanations to be sufficient.
results.fragility: At the held-out tier the exclusion is one-way and narrow (0.012), and P-1128's printed validation interval is narrower than HM would give (about 0.776-0.984 at 21/29). P-1128's other models' validation intervals contain 0.805: network-clinical 0.783-0.915 and morphology 0.672-0.896. The declared best model is the one compared. P-13's optimism-corrected 0.829 lies inside P-1128's validation interval. The both-way exclusion at the headline (apparent) tier, z = 5.67, does not depend on any of this.
results.reason: Same question (ADNI MCI-to-AD conversion from MRI plus clinical data, C-index), and no matched figure: P-13's single-timepoint figures in the subgroup are lower still. Each paper's headline estimate (0.844, 0.815-0.873; 0.951, 0.928-0.974) lies outside the other's printed interval (z = 5.67). At the held-out tier, P-13's 0.805 lies outside P-1128's printed 0.817-0.943, which is condition 4 as worded. Every condition is met.
